Fairfax County and its cities

Virginia's most populous county is Fairfax, mostly suburban, on the Virginia side of the Potomac opposite Washington, D.C. It had 1,150,309 residents in 2020 and covers 406 square miles.

The City of Fairfax is the county seat, but under Virginia law it is an independent city and is not part of the county. Falls Church and Alexandria are independent cities too, which is why a Fairfax County tax bill never covers a house inside those city limits. A house with a Fairfax mailing address might be billed by the county or by the City of Fairfax, or carry a Town of Herndon charge on top of the county. Check the name on the bill before you call anyone.

The Department of Tax Administration has collected the Town of Herndon's current real estate tax since a March 8, 2022 agreement, so Herndon owners get one bill that carries both the county and the town charge.

Tax rate and district charges

The county lists the 2026 base real estate rate at $1.12 per $100 of assessed value. The same page shows $1.1225 for 2025 and $1.125 for 2024. The Board of Supervisors sets the general rate in early May each year.

Not every parcel pays the same extra charges. Find your parcel's tax district number in the county's assessment lookup, then match it against the 2026 rate chart. The assessment notice also shows which service districts apply.

Tysons Service District$0.05 per $100

The county also lists a $959 yearly charge for Springfield Water Service District 3, which runs through December 31, 2032 and serves a small group of homes in the Lincoln-Lewis-Vannoy Conservation District. Commercial transportation and Dulles Rail districts apply to commercial property, not to a typical house.

Due dates and penalties

Fairfax County bills real estate tax in two installments: July 28 and December 5. A due date on a weekend or county holiday rolls to the next business day, which is why the December 2026 installment falls on Monday, December 7, 2026.

  • End of February: Notice of Real Estate Assessment Change mailed.
  • April 1: deadline for an appeal to the Department of Tax Administration.
  • June 1: deadline for an appeal to the Board of Equalization.
  • July 28: first installment due. Bills go out by June 30.
  • December 5: second installment due. Bills go out by November 5.

An appeal does not pause the due date. Late payment brings penalties and interest even while the appeal is open, and the office can give you the current penalty figure.

How to appeal your assessment

There are three levels. The assessment effective date is January 1, and the county reported an average residential increase of 3.99% for 2026.

  1. Department of Tax Administration review. File by April 1 (postmarked, or 4:30 p.m. if online or by email). Mail goes to 12000 Government Center Parkway, Suite 357, Fairfax, VA 22035.
  2. Board of Equalization, an independent panel appointed by the Board of Supervisors. File by June 1. Its decisions are final but can be taken to circuit court.
  3. Fairfax County Circuit Court, through an Application for Correction of Erroneous Assessment under Virginia Code 58.1-3984.

A valid appeal rests on fair market value, lack of uniformity or an error in the property description. A one-year jump that simply feels too large is not a legal basis. For a house, bring comparable sales. If an agent files for you, they need a signed, notarized authorization letter.

Appraisal staff take calls at 703-222-8234 on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Selling with unpaid tax

A tax debt stays attached to the house. In Virginia the lien for real estate tax ranks first until the money is actually paid, and Virginia Code 58.1-3340 directs sale proceeds to taxes and levies on the property, penalties and interest included. A second lien also reaches the current year's rents.

Your contract prorates the seller's share of the year. When an installment is open at closing, ask the settlement agent to show you how it will appear on the closing statement.

The deed carries a seller-side charge as well. Under Virginia Code 58.1-802, the grantor's tax is 50 cents per $500 of consideration. The grantor pays unless both sides agree the buyer takes some or all of it, and the deed's first page must state the consideration.

Relief and damaged houses

Seniors 65 and older and people with disabilities can apply for county tax relief, and exemptions exist for disabled service members and certain surviving spouses. Renewals are due May 1. First-time and hardship applicants can file through December 31 for the current year and one prior year.

A damaged or decayed house has its own route. The county can adjust the assessment when a building is wholly destroyed, or reduced in value below $100 by decay, or impaired by violence by $100 or more, under Virginia Code 58.1-3293. Any adjustment is prorated from the incident until the repair or the end of the year. Send the address or tax map number, a description of the damage, repair estimates if you have them and photographs to the Department of Tax Administration at 703-222-8234.

What the district charges mean for a buyer

Two houses on the same street can carry different yearly bills because of the districts they sit in. A buyer's lender will add the base rate and any district charges, so a house in Tysons, Reston or Lake Barcroft may cost more to hold than a similar house outside those areas. A refuse fee or leaf collection charge applies only in some districts.

Give a buyer the tax district number from the assessment lookup and a copy of your latest notice. It saves a round of questions and makes your price easier to defend.

Steps before you sell

Pull your latest assessment notice and list the district charges that apply to your parcel. Confirm who bills you (the county, the City of Fairfax or the Town of Herndon) and which installment is paid. A figure that looks wrong deserves a call to 703-222-8234. Then ask the settlement agent how the unpaid balance and the grantor tax will appear on the closing statement.

If the house is damaged, start the adjustment request before you list. If you would rather not repair it, a direct as-is cash offer skips showings and lender approvals, and any tax owed is paid from the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Is Fairfax County property tax paid once or twice a year?

Twice a year. The first installment is due July 28 and the second December 5, moved to Monday, December 7 in 2026 because December 5 falls on a Saturday.

What is the Fairfax County base real estate tax rate?

The county lists $1.12 per $100 of assessed value for tax year 2026. Your notice shows any district charges on top.

What are the Fairfax County assessment appeal deadlines?

April 1 for the Department of Tax Administration and June 1 for the Board of Equalization. Keep paying on time while any appeal is pending.

Who collects tax for the Town of Herndon?

Fairfax County's Department of Tax Administration does, under a March 8, 2022 agreement. Herndon owners receive one combined bill for county and town real estate tax.

Does the buyer or the seller pay the Virginia grantor's tax?

The seller, as grantor, pays it unless both sides agree that the buyer covers some or all of it. The rate under Virginia Code 58.1-802 is 50 cents for each $500 of consideration.

Loudoun County in brief

Loudoun is a northern Virginia county on the Potomac, across from Maryland, and part of the Washington metro area. Its seat, Leesburg, is also its biggest town. The 2020 census counted 420,959 residents and the 2025 estimate is 449,749. Growth was fast: 86,129 people in 1990, 169,599 in 2000 and 312,311 in 2010.

With so few empty homes, most sellers here own houses built in the last few decades, although the western towns hold much older ones. Median household income is high, but a job loss, divorce or inherited property still pushes owners to sell quickly.

East and west sell differently

The county has seven incorporated towns: Hamilton, Hillsboro, Leesburg, Lovettsville, Middleburg, Purcellville and Round Hill. A house inside a town sits under town government as well as the county, so ask the town office about local rules for your street.

Ashburn, South Riding, Sterling, Brambleton, Broadlands, Stone Ridge, Lansdowne, Sugarland Run, Cascades, Lowes Island and Countryside are large census-designated places in the east, and Waterford, Aldie, Bluemont and Lucketts anchor the rural west. The eastern planned communities are recent subdivisions. The Loudoun Valley mixes villages, farms and horse properties. A roof, septic system or well on a rural lot gets different scrutiny than a townhouse on public utilities, so price and market each accordingly.

Buyers also raise commuting. U.S. 15, U.S. 50, U.S. 340 and State Routes 7, 9, 28 and 267 (the Dulles Greenway) are the main roads, and the Metro Silver Line serves the Dulles Airport, Loudoun Gateway and Ashburn stations. Mention a nearby station, toll road or flight path when you describe the house.

Who does what for real estate tax

Assessments come from the Commissioner of the Revenue. Bills and payments run through the Treasurer. Deeds are recorded by the elected Clerk of the Circuit Court. Call these offices for the current installment dates, rate and penalty figures before you plan a sale.

Schools also come up. Loudoun County Public Schools serves more than 70,000 students, and attendance zones depend on the address, so send buyers to the school division and not a listing.

Correcting or contesting an assessment

State law gives owners two routes that apply in every county. If the problem is clerical or factual, ask the assessing officer for a correction. The window is three years past the end of the tax year, or one year after the assessment date, whichever falls later, and it reaches mistakes by the assessing office and factual errors from a general reassessment. See Virginia Code 58.1-3980.

Disagreements about value go to the board of equalization, which presumes the assessor is right. The board may consider market sales through the December 31 before the assessment date if they are filed by the locality's deadline.

  • Pull sold prices for similar homes close to yours.
  • Take pictures of flaws an assessor could not see from the road.
  • Compare the record's square footage and room counts with the real house.

If you are behind on tax

With good cause, a locality can pass a resolution giving reasonable extensions of up to 90 days on real estate tax. State law also requires an automatic extension on a primary residence for service members deployed outside the United States, ending 90 days after deployment ends.

For taxes that were omitted and later assessed, an authorized Treasurer can set up a plan of up to 72 months, provided current taxes keep being paid on time. Penalties top out at 10 percent of the tax past due, and the starting interest rate is capped at 10 percent a year.

Penalty and interest are barred when the late payment was not your fault, for example certain postal errors, and the Treasurer is the one who judges fault, so raise it early.

Selling with taxes owed

Whatever tax remains unpaid gets cleared from your proceeds at signing, so the Treasurer's payoff figure is your first request. Put it in writing for the title company, and check whether a program on the parcel, such as a use-value arrangement, stops after the sale.

  1. Get the Treasurer's balance and the date through which it holds.
  2. Have the Commissioner of the Revenue verify the details on your record.
  3. Forward both to the closing agent.
  4. Confirm afterward that the account shows paid.

Before you list a Loudoun house

Three short calls head off most tax surprises. Begin with the Treasurer, who can tell you the balance, the next installment and what penalty or interest has been added. Move on to the Commissioner of the Revenue and confirm that the record matches the house: finished basement, bedroom count, square footage and lot size. A wrong detail can inflate the value a buyer's agent sees when they look you up.

If your home sits inside Leesburg, Purcellville, Middleburg or another town, ask the town office what applies on top of county rules. Learning about any extra town rule before you list saves time.

Locate permits for every deck, basement finish or addition. Loudoun buyers tend to be careful and well informed, and an unpermitted improvement is a common reason a closing slips.

How tax is divided when you close

On closing day someone has to cover the stretch between the last payment and the settlement date. Your contract names who pays what, and the settlement agent turns that into credits and charges. Review the proration line with the agent, and ask them to show the dates they used.

Should a bill arrive after the sale, the Treasurer may reissue it to the new owner, who then has two weeks from that notice to pay penalty-free. Even so, make sure your own tax is current at closing. A seller who carries a balance into settlement will see it taken from the proceeds, and interest keeps adding until the day it is paid.

Take photo ID and parcel details to settlement. When the owner has died, the person with court authority brings that paperwork too.

What a cash sale changes

Without a lender's appraisal or loan approval, a cash purchase takes out a common cause of delay. The tax lien stays, though. No matter who buys, the balance comes out of the proceeds, and the Treasurer still supplies the exact payoff.

Cash offers suit houses that need work, carry tenants or belong to an estate. Weigh the offer against what a listing would net after repairs, agent costs and months of carrying the house, and do not rush. Because a deployed service member gets an extension on a primary residence, ask the Treasurer about that rule if it applies to you.

Who sets real estate assessments in Loudoun County?

The Commissioner of the Revenue's office handles assessments, while the Treasurer bills and collects.

How big is Loudoun County, Virginia?

The county covers 521 square miles and had 420,959 residents in the 2020 census, making it Virginia's third most populous county.

Is Loudoun County mostly owner-occupied?

Yes. The 2020 census shows 76.4 percent of occupied housing units were owner-occupied and 23.6 percent were rented.

Can I get a Loudoun County property tax penalty removed?

Virginia law bars penalty and interest when the failure to pay was not the taxpayer's fault, such as certain postal errors. Ask the Treasurer, who decides fault for late payments.

Which office to contact

Tax Administration houses two offices. The Real Estate Assessments Office sets values, and Taxpayer Services handles bills and payments.

OfficeWhat it doesHow to reach it

Walk-in hours at the assessment office are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday to Friday, and phones are staffed from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Pay through the county's Taxpayer Portal. Check washing fraud is the reason the county advises against sending checks in the mail.

Due dates

Two installments make up the annual bill. Recent notices have set the first half at July 15 and the second at December 5.

Taxpayer Services can confirm this year's exact dates, which is worth doing before you schedule a closing. Owners with mortgages mostly pay through escrow. Servicing companies are billed directly by the county, so a paper bill that lands in your mailbox by mistake should be forwarded to your servicer.

Improvements completed after the year begins can draw a supplemental real estate tax. An addition or a finished basement from the past year is worth asking about.

How the bill is figured

The formula is simple: assessed value over 100, times the total rate quoted per $100.

Several layers go into that total. Each year the Board of County Supervisors fixes a countywide base rate. Levies for Fire and Rescue and for Mosquito and Forest Pest Management come on top, as do special district levies that fund items like road improvements. Storm water management and solid waste are charged as separate fees. Your address decides which layers apply, so rely on the rate printed on your bill.

  • Look up which special district levies cover your address.
  • Include storm water and solid waste fees when your bill lists them.
  • Ask whether new construction triggers a supplemental bill.

How to challenge your assessment

Take it to the Real Estate Assessments Office first. Still unresolved? Next comes the Board of Equalization, and after that the circuit court.

Under the county's Taxpayer Bill of Rights you may look at the working papers behind your value, sit down with assessment staff and request a correction when the value seems wrong or unfair. Your notice and the office can tell you which dates and steps apply.

Va. Code 58.1-3379 sets the ground rules for the board. It presumes the assessor is right, and the burden falls on you to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, either that the value tops fair market value or that the assessment is not uniform. Evidence of sales and income through the December 31 before the assessment date is allowed.

Va. Code 58.1-3980 offers another path: ask the assessing official to fix an erroneous assessment, within three years after the tax year ends or one year after the assessment, whichever comes later. It addresses mistakes by the assessor, not disputes over opinion of value.

Selling with taxes owed

Back tax stays with the property, since the lien outranks all others until paid.

Under Va. Code 58.1-3340, a buyer or foreclosure trustee has to see that sale proceeds go toward every tax assessed on the real estate, with penalties and interest counted. Contract terms divide the year between you and the buyer, and the treasurer or another proper officer then lifts the lien. The closing agent normally pays the balance from your proceeds. Request a payoff from Taxpayer Services that covers the current half, and do it before a closing date is chosen.

A grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of consideration is imposed by Va. Code 58.1-802. Sellers owe it unless the contract assigns it to the buyer, and no deed gets recorded before it is paid. One Circuit Court clerk serves the county, Manassas and Manassas Park, so a single office takes recording questions for all three.

Is your house in the county or a city?

Manassas, the county seat, is an independent city located inside the county, and Manassas Park is another that the county surrounds. Homes in either one get their bills from the city rather than the county. Look at the town named on your deed before searching for a tax account. Confirm the jurisdiction on your bill if you are unsure.

Out west, a green belt known as the rural crescent covers much of the county, and it can affect any parcel bigger than a subdivision lot.

The Prince William market

Homeownership is the norm. The 2020 count was 158,525 housing units with 3.0 percent vacant, and 71.6 percent of occupied units were owner-occupied. The market is tied to commuting into Washington, D.C., and to military employers such as Marine Corps Base Quantico.

Owners who are behind, who inherited a house or who face repairs sometimes choose a direct cash sale, which skips repair demands from retail buyers. The lien must still be cleared at closing, so the same payoff steps apply.

Before you contact the county

Have your parcel or account number and the property address in front of you. If you are asking for a correction, note exactly what you think is wrong, for example the square footage, the finished space or the condition, and gather photos or a contractor's estimate to support it. Staff can only act on specifics. For a billing question, find your most recent bill so the representative can see what has been posted. Emailing first leaves a written record, and the phone line is better for urgent payoff requests.

Allow time for the answer. A request sent the week before closing may not come back before the closing date, so ask early and say plainly that a sale is pending.

Steps before you close

Order a payoff from Taxpayer Services covering the current half. See whether recent improvements could produce a supplemental bill. Tell the closing agent which jurisdiction bills the parcel. Read the proration wording so the July 15 and December 5 installments are divided as you expect. Last, ask your servicer how much of the balance escrow already holds, so the payoff and any escrow refund match on the settlement statement. Call each office a few days before closing to confirm that nothing has changed, since a balance can shift when a payment posts or a bill is issued. Bring a photo ID to any in-person visit.

Frequently asked questions

When are Prince William County real estate taxes due?

Recent notices put the first half at July 15 and the second at December 5. Taxpayer Services can confirm this year's dates.

Who do I call about a Prince William County assessment?

The Real Estate Assessments Office at 703-792-6780 or realestate@pwcgov.org. For billing and payment questions, call Taxpayer Services at 703-792-6710.

Can I sell my Prince William County house if I owe property tax?

Yes, it comes out of your proceeds at closing since the lien has priority. A payoff figure from Taxpayer Services lets the closing agent add penalties and interest correctly.

Does Prince William County bill houses in Manassas?

No. Manassas and Manassas Park are independent cities surrounded by the county and bill their own real estate tax. Confirm the jurisdiction on your deed or bill.

What can I do if I think my Prince William County value is too high?

Request a review from the Real Estate Assessments Office, and if needed appeal to the Board of Equalization or the circuit court. Bring sales or appraisal evidence, because the assessor is presumed correct.

Chesterfield County at a glance

Chesterfield County lies directly south of Richmond, with the James River along much of its northern edge and the Appomattox River along much of its southern one. The county seat is Chesterfield Court House, and there are no incorporated towns. The 2020 census counted 364,548 residents, the fourth most populous county in Virginia, and the county's 2025 estimate is 397,148. It covers 437 square miles.

Postwar commuter growth built much of the county, which means many houses are decades old. Tired roofs, older HVAC systems and dated kitchens often keep a listing from selling, and a lender-backed buyer may demand repairs that a cash buyer will not.

Communities include Chester, Midlothian, Bon Air, Brandermill, Ettrick, Bermuda Hundred and Matoaca, and the northern part is often called North Chesterfield. Ettrick lies in Chesterfield but is mostly served by a Petersburg mailing address. A seller there should ask the county tax office, not rely on the postal city, to learn which locality bills the parcel.

Assessments and the tax rate

Chesterfield reassesses real estate every year. Notices are mailed by February 1 and show values as of January 1. The county says assessments must reflect 100 percent of fair market value, based on inspections, sales data and comparisons with similar nearby properties.

The Board of Supervisors sets the tax rate. The county lists $0.89 per $100 of assessed value for 2026.

How to appeal your assessment

Two filings, in order: Real Estate Assessments by March 15, then the Board of Equalization by April 15. Late applications are not processed, and you cannot skip the first level.

  1. Review your values on the county's READ site or contact the office.
  2. Get the application and file a separate one for each property.
  3. Attach support: up to three comparable properties, a recent appraisal or photos, and for income property three years of income and expense statements plus a current rent roll.
  4. If a representative files for you, add a notarized Letter of Authorization.
  5. An appraiser may ask questions or inspect, then notifies you of the outcome.

State code makes the Board of Equalization independent: a Circuit Court judge names its members and the state tax department trains them. Under 58.1-3379, the assessor's value is presumed correct and the owner must rebut it. Real Estate Assessments is at 6801 Mimms Loop, phone 804-748-1321, email assessor@chesterfield.gov.

The Treasurer's Office is at 9901 Lori Road, Room 101, Chesterfield, VA 23832, with mail to P.O. Box 70. The phone is 804-748-1201, and hours are weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

How Henrico assesses real estate

The county revalues each parcel yearly, at 100 percent of fair market value, and the figure takes effect January 1. The Real Estate Assessment Division, part of the Department of Finance, works from recorded deeds and the sale prices that buyers, sellers and agents report.

Staff compare sale prices with assessed values, and a neighborhood is picked for reassessment when its ratio sits well above or below 100 percent. For houses the division generally uses the sales comparison approach, adjusting for size, quality, condition and location.

Notices are mailed beginning in February. Tax bills often go straight to the mortgage company, so an owner with an escrow account may never see the notice unless the lender forwards it; look up your value on the division's page at henrico.gov.

Start by applying for reconsideration. State law makes April 1 of the current year the final filing day. Call 804-501-4300 or write to AssessmentAppeal@henrico.gov for forms.

Staff inspect the property, tell you the value they recommend and send the case to the Board of Real Estate Review and Equalization. If you still disagree, you may appear before the board.

The county's GIS-Web viewer shows assessment data and is the place to confirm that your parcel is in the county before you look up a bill.

Growth areas and rural land

The county's comprehensive plan steers new development into Development Areas, which make up about 5 percent of the county. The rest is Rural Area meant for agriculture, natural resource protection and some homes. The Board of Supervisors adopted the current plan, AC44, on October 15, 2025.

Arlington at a glance

Arlington is a small, fully urban county directly across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. It covers about 26 square miles and borders Fairfax County, the City of Falls Church and the City of Alexandria. The 2020 census counted 238,643 residents.

Rosslyn, Clarendon, Ballston, Pentagon City and Court House are the neighborhoods people name most often. Four Metro lines (Orange, Blue, Silver and Yellow) serve the county, and Interstates 395 and 66 cross it. Arlington assesses every parcel as of January 1 each year, so the number on your notice is the starting point for any question about your tax, wherever the house sits.

Due dates and penalties

Arlington bills real estate tax in two equal installments. When a due date lands on a weekend or holiday, paying on the next business day keeps you clear of the penalty.

InstallmentDue dateIf paid late
First halfJune 15State cap: 10 percent penalty, 10 percent yearly interest
Second halfOctober 5State cap: 10 percent penalty, 10 percent yearly interest

Virginia law puts the burden on you to know the dates. A missing bill is no defense for paying late. A few cases come up often:

  • Escrow accounts: your lender pays, and you hear from the Treasurer's Office only if that payment never arrives.
  • Already sold: if a bill for the old address reaches you after the buyer took over, return it to the Treasurer's Office along with whatever you know about the new owner.
  • Moving: send your new billing address to the Department of Real Estate Assessments in writing.

The real estate tax rate

For calendar year 2025 the rate was $1.033 per $100 of assessed value. Commercial property, such as office buildings and hotels, pays an extra $0.125 per $100. The County Board sets the rate each April, and a later year's rate may differ, so use the figure printed on your current bill.

A buyer's lender will look at your assessed value and this rate to size the yearly tax. Check both before you set an asking price, and ask the Department of Real Estate Assessments if anything on the notice is unclear.

How Arlington assesses your house

Assessments take effect as of January 1 each year and are mailed and posted online each January. The county defines fair market value as what the property would bring in a normal sale.

The county uses a 12-month sales period that starts 16 months before the effective date. It studies all the sales in a neighborhood, so a single sale has only a diluted effect on your value. If your neighbor's house sold for far more or less than yours is assessed, that one sale alone will not move your number much.

When you are getting ready to sell, set the assessed value next to what local agents think a buyer will pay. A large gap either way is a reason to phone the assessment office.

How to appeal your assessment

There are four steps, and you can skip some of them. Each has its own deadline.

  • Start by speaking with a neighborhood appraiser at 703-228-3920 or assessments@arlingtonva.us.
  • File a Department Review Request. The county gives March 1 in one place and March 2 in another, so use the date printed on your notice.
  • The Board of Equalization takes filings through April 15. Its seven members are county residents appointed each year, and it operates apart from the assessment office.
  • Sue in Circuit Court at 1425 North Courthouse Road, phone 703-228-7010, which is the final option.

No determination letter by April 1? File with the board anyway so you do not lose the option. Going straight to the board, with no department review first, is also allowed. A review can lower the value, confirm it or raise it.

A department review begins when an appraiser calls to set up an inspection, normally of the interior and exterior with a second appraiser along. The appraiser writes a recommendation, a supervisor reviews it, and the Director of Real Estate Assessments makes the final call, with written notice by mail or email. Declining the inspection, or withdrawing, is allowed, but the review then relies on the records the county already holds. A person filing on your behalf needs your signed letter of authorization.

Tax relief for seniors and disabled owners

Through its Real Estate Tax Relief Program, the county offers an exemption or a deferral to owners aged 65 and up, and to owners who are totally and permanently disabled. The filing deadline is November 15.

The county listed 2025 limits of annual income up to $105,937 and assets, not counting the home, up to $499,709 for an exemption or $674,606 for a deferral. A separate exemption covers a veteran rated 100 percent disabled by a permanent, total, service-connected condition, and a surviving spouse may qualify. The limits get revised, so check with the county before you file.

What happens to the tax bill when you sell?

Decide who owes what at the closing table. The Treasurer's Office expects the tax responsibility to be sorted out at settlement, and your settlement attorney can walk you through it.

Unpaid tax attaches to the property itself under Virginia Code section 58.1-3340 and stands first in line among liens. Your sale contract decides how the current year's bill is split. The state ceiling on a late penalty is 10 percent of the overdue tax or $10, whichever is larger, and the interest ceiling is 10 percent a year.

Deed costs are separate. The grantor tax in section 58.1-802 runs 50 cents per $500 and usually falls to the seller. The state recordation tax in section 58.1-801 is 25 cents per $100.

In order: find out from the Treasurer's Office what is paid and what is open, hand your settlement attorney the installment dates, and get the final split on paper before closing.

Before you list: a short checklist

Collect your January assessment notice, your most recent bill and your mortgage servicer's name. If the value looks wrong, phone the Department of Real Estate Assessments at 703-228-3920, and remember April 15 if you plan to contest it at the board. Confirm with the Treasurer's Office which installments are paid so the year can be prorated correctly.

If you are 65 or older, or totally and permanently disabled, ask whether the relief program applies to you. An exemption or deferral affects what the next owner takes on.

Selling for cash

Some Arlington owners skip the listing process. The usual reasons: repairs they would rather not fund, tax or a loan running behind, or a move on a short clock. With two installments a year, a missed June or October payment can pile up fast on a vacant house.

Cash Home Buyers makes written cash offers on houses in their current condition, so nothing needs fixing first and there are no open houses. Send the address by call or text. Hold any offer, ours included, up against the January 1 value on your notice before you decide.

Frequently asked questions

When are Arlington County real estate taxes due?

June 15 and October 5. If a date falls on a weekend or holiday, paying the next business day avoids the penalty.

What was Arlington's real estate tax rate for 2025?

$1.033 per $100 of assessed value, plus $0.125 per $100 for commercial property. The County Board sets the rate each April.

What is the deadline to appeal an Arlington assessment to the Board of Equalization?

April 15. Forms must be delivered, postmarked or filed online by midnight that day.

Who do I call about my Arlington assessment?

The Department of Real Estate Assessments at 703-228-3920, at 2100 Clarendon Blvd, Suite 502, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Meetings are by appointment.

Can I get tax relief in Arlington if I am over 65?

Possibly. The Real Estate Tax Relief Program covers owners 65 and older and those totally and permanently disabled, subject to income and asset limits. The filing deadline is November 15.

Hanover County in brief

Hanover lies about 12 miles up the road from Richmond and about 90 miles below Washington, D.C. The seat is Hanover Courthouse, Ashland is the only incorporated town, and Mechanicsville is the largest census-designated place. Older farmhouses and village homes near Ashland and the courthouse mix with postwar subdivisions around Mechanicsville, so age and condition vary a lot from one road to the next.

With 82 percent of occupied homes lived in by their owners, most sellers here are individual homeowners rather than landlords.

Who handles the tax

Hanover has an elected Commissioner of the Revenue, an elected Treasurer and a Clerk of the Circuit Court. Think of three desks. The assessing office puts a number on your house, the Treasurer mails the bill and takes the check, and the Clerk files the deed once you sell. Call the Treasurer and the assessing office for current installment dates and rates before you rely on any date you have read elsewhere.

Questions worth asking on that call:

  • What is the balance on my parcel, and does it include penalty or interest?
  • Which installment is next, and when does the penalty start?
  • By what date must an appeal of this year's value be filed?
  • If we close after a bill is mailed, can it be reissued in the buyer's name?

How a Virginia assessment appeal works

The local board of equalization assumes the assessor got it right, which leaves the proving to you. To prevail, show with a preponderance of the evidence that the house is carried above fair market value, or that the assessment is uneven and set against accepted appraisal practice.

Homes with fewer than four units come with extra protections. The assessing officer owes you written notice, and a written request gets you the assessment records within 15 days. Evidence has limits too: sales up to December 31 before the effective date count if they reach the board by the locality's deadline, and later-published studies do not.

A strong file holds recent comparable sales, photos of defects and proof of factual errors, wrong square footage being the classic one. The statute treats mistakes of fact, computation errors included, as a departure from accepted practice. See the rule at Virginia Code 58.1-3379.

When a house sells after the bill is mailed

Say the deed changes hands just after bills are mailed. The Treasurer may void the old owner's copy and send a new one to the buyer, and if the buyer pays within two weeks of that reissued notice, no penalty can be added to that assessment.

A late penalty on real estate tops out at 10 percent of the tax past due, interest is limited to 10 percent a year during the first year (a different ceiling follows), and collection fees a locality has contracted for can reach 20 percent of the delinquent amount. Hanover's own numbers come from county ordinance, which the Treasurer can quote.

Deed tax at closing

Recording a deed costs money separately. The grantor's tax is 50 cents on every $500 of value, billed to the seller unless the contract puts it on the buyer. Before a deed can be recorded the Clerk has to certify payment, and the proceeds are shared by the state and the locality. See Virginia Code 58.1-802.

On settlement day any unpaid real estate tax also comes out of your proceeds, so ask the Treasurer for a payoff quote in advance and avoid a shock on the statement.

What to have ready for a sale

Hanover sellers can save a week or more by pulling paperwork before a contract arrives. Keep the latest assessment notice, your most recent tax bills with their account numbers and, for an inherited house, the deed or will and any court order naming the person who can sign. Gather any receipts for roof, septic or drainage work as well, since inspectors in a county with both old farm properties and postwar subdivisions tend to dig into those systems.

Interstates 95 and 295 cross the county, and many residents commute toward Richmond, so buyers will ask about drive times and which road your street connects to.   2. Decide whether this year's value is worth challenging, and if so, collect comparable sales and photos now, since the board accepts only evidence that reaches it by the locality's deadline.
  3. Ask whether any bill already mailed will need to be reissued after closing.
  4. Choose a closing agent and share the payoff and any deed-tax questions in writing.
  5. Once the deed is recorded, ask the Treasurer to confirm the account is paid.

Hanover's mix of rural lots and subdivision homes means the time to sell can swing widely. A neat lot near Ashland or Mechanicsville may draw several showings in a week, while a farmhouse down a country road may wait. Price with that in mind, and tell your agent or buyer about any known issue with a well, septic system or fence line before the inspection does.

A cash sale compresses that list, since there is no lender to wait on, but the tax and the deed levy are handled the same way.

If your tax bill is behind

Behind on tax? You have three realistic routes. Pay from the sale proceeds, ask the Treasurer about an extension or payment plan, or sell to someone who will take the house as it is. A locality may grant extensions of up to 90 days by resolution when good cause exists. A taxpayer who misses a deadline because of a death or a documented medical impairment is presumed to be without fault if payment comes within 30 days.

An assessment under administrative appeal also gets breathing room. An appeal filed within 90 days of the assessment shields the bill from delinquency while the case is open and for 30 days after the final ruling.

Inherited, vacant or worn-out houses

A lot of Hanover sales start with a home left vacant after a death, or an aging place needing major repairs. Get the payoff first. Then the person with legal authority to sell should collect the deed and court papers a title company will want.

Cash Home Buyers will tour the house in whatever shape it is in and explain how any tax balance gets cleared when you close. The county Treasurer sends and collects the bill. The Commissioner of the Revenue and the assessing office handle values.

Call the assessing office for this year's deadline. Under Virginia law the owner must show the value is too high or not uniform.

Can penalties on Hanover County property tax be waived?

Virginia law bars penalty and interest when the failure was not the taxpayer's fault, including certain postal errors, and presumes no fault after a death or medical impairment when payment follows within 30 days. The Treasurer decides fault for late payments.

Who pays the Virginia deed tax when selling a house in Hanover County?

The seller, as grantor, pays the state grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 unless the contract assigns some of it to the buyer. The Clerk of the Circuit Court collects it at recording.

Caroline County overview

Caroline County lies in eastern Virginia, bounded on the north by the Rappahannock River. The 2020 census counted 30,887 residents on 537 square miles, roughly twice the figure from fifty years before, so a lot of the housing is newer construction mixed into old farm country.

The county seat, Bowling Green, is also its largest town, and Port Royal is the only other incorporated one. A good share of residents work outside the county. Interstate 95 passes through with exits 104 and 110, and U.S. Routes 1, 17 and 301 cross the county as well. When buyers look at a Caroline house they weigh the drive along I-95 almost as much as the lot, and a property near an exit is easier to market than one down a long rural lane.

Caroline bills in two parts. A late payment picks up penalty and interest the next day, and personal property and business personal property follow the same calendar.

InstallmentDue datePenalty and interest added
First halfJune 5June 6: 10 percent penalty and 10 percent interest

State law draws the outer boundaries. Code of Virginia 58.1-3916 lets a locality charge up to 10 percent a year in interest and up to 10 percent of the overdue tax as a penalty. A locality may waive both if the lateness was not the taxpayer's doing, or if a timely mailed payment carried proof of mailing and showed up within five days of the deadline.

Who to call: Treasurer and Commissioner

Your tax runs through two desks. Payments go to the Treasurer, and the Commissioner of the Revenue deals with assessment questions.

  • Treasurer: 212 N Main Street, Bowling Green, VA 22427, 804-633-5291, weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Payments by mail go to P.O. Box 431.
  • Commissioner's real estate office: 804-633-9834 or realestate@co.caroline.va.us.

How to check or appeal your assessment

Look up your parcel in the Real Estate Assessment Information tool at caroline.civ.quest or on the Tax Map page, then call the Commissioner's real estate office. If that does not settle it, the Board of Equalization is next.

In a reassessment year, concerned owners are heard first by the Board of Assessors. A Board of Equalization is then seated for complaints. It has six citizen members who are nominated by the Board of Supervisors, approved by a Circuit Court judge and trained through the state tax department. Once it rules, the final route is a petition to Circuit Court under Section 58.1-3984.

Know the burden before you file. Section 58.1-3379 assumes the assessor got it right, so you must prove the value exceeds fair market value, was applied unevenly, or was set outside accepted appraisal practice. For a home with fewer than four units, a written request for the assessment records must be answered within 15 days.

  • Water. The county names the Carmel Church Ladysmith, Milford, Port Royal and Townfield systems. Public Utilities is at 804-633-4390.
  • Senior and disability relief. Call the real estate office at 804-633-9834.

On the deed, the grantor tax in 58.1-802 is 50 cents per $500 of value. The statute assigns it to the seller, and the two sides can agree to shift it.

Miss December 5 and the balance grows by December 6, when penalty and interest are added. The payoff at closing ends up bigger than the original bill.

Request the balance for your expected closing date and have the closing agent verify it. Proceeds cover the open amount. When repairs would scare off an ordinary buyer, an as-is purchase spares you the fix-up and the showings.

A standard listing in Caroline County usually means permit cleanup, repairs, photos, showings and a wait for the buyer's lender. A direct as-is sale cuts most of that. You still owe the same tax, and the Treasurer's payoff is still the number that matters, but you are not paying carrying costs while the house sits on the market. Each month of waiting also adds to the risk of a missed bill, since penalty and interest arrive the day after a due date.

If you want to compare routes, ask an agent for a net-proceeds estimate and ask us for a written offer. Set both against the Treasurer's payoff and decide which leaves you better off.

A short checklist before you sell

Ring the Treasurer at 804-633-5291 for a payoff and the paid-installment history. Reach the real estate office at 804-633-9834 if the assessment seems off or you want the parcel records. Walk through the house looking for open permits or half-finished work, since a buyer's inspector or lender may ask about them. If the land sits in the preservation program, ask the Commissioner's office how a sale affects it.

Give your closing agent the written payoff plus the split you agreed for this year. The balance is then taken from your proceeds when the deed is recorded.

If you are a senior or have a disability, check whether the relief program reduces what a buyer will owe. That can change a buyer's calculation of the yearly cost, and the real estate office is the place to ask about it.

What are the Caroline County tax due dates?

June 5 and December 5. Penalty and interest of 10 percent each begin the following day.

Visit 212 N Main Street in Bowling Green on weekdays between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., call 804-633-5291, or write to P.O. Box 431, Bowling Green, VA 22427.

What is the appeal process for a Caroline County assessment?

Call the Commissioner's real estate office, take any unresolved dispute to the Board of Equalization, and as a last resort petition Circuit Court under Section 58.1-3984.

Can I sell if I owe back taxes in Caroline County?

Usually. The open balance is paid from your proceeds at closing. Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer and have the closing agent double-check it.

The seller, by default, at 50 cents per $500. Buyer and seller can agree that the buyer covers some or all of it.

Augusta County and its two cities

Augusta County sits in the Shenandoah Valley on the western side of Virginia. The 2020 census counted 77,487 residents, and most of them live in unincorporated communities such as Stuarts Draft, Fishersville and Verona rather than in a town. Craigsville and Grottoes are the two towns.

The county completely surrounds the independent cities of Staunton and Waynesboro, but those cities are separate localities. A house with a Staunton or Waynesboro mailing address may be taxed by the city, while a house just outside the line is taxed by Augusta County. The community name on a mailing label does not decide who bills you. The parcel's location does, so check the county's online assessment records or call the offices before you assume.

Sellers in Stuarts Draft, Fishersville, Verona, Weyers Cave, Crimora or Churchville all deal with the same county offices. Buyers coming from Staunton or Waynesboro often assume the rates and billing match their old city, and they do not, so expect questions about the county bill during negotiation.

Due dates and penalties

Augusta splits the annual bill into two equal halves. A due date that lands on a weekend slides to the Monday after, and owners who prefer one payment can pay everything in June. The county's e-Treasurer site lets you look up and pay a bill online.

InstallmentDue dateLate charge

The Board of Supervisors set the 2024 rate at $0.52 per $100 of assessed value, and the Real Estate Assessor's Office values every parcel as of January 1. The penalty applies to the unpaid balance. Interest does not run on the state's share of personal property tax.

Taxpayers are expected to know the due dates. If no bill arrives, contact the taxing office before the date to arrange payment.

When the late charge is waived

The county does not accept these as reasons: you did not know the due date, no bill came, the bill went to a wrong address, the bill was wrong, or a staff member gave bad information. A waiver is possible only in narrower cases:

  • A medically determinable physical or mental impairment on the due date, with payment made within 30 days.
  • The Commissioner of Revenue abates the tax or certifies a clerical error by that office.
  • The late payment was caused solely by the Treasurer or the Commissioner of Revenue.

If you cannot pay the whole amount, ask the Treasurer's Office about a payment plan at (540) 245-5660 or treasurer@co.augusta.va.us. The plan leaves the penalty in place, and interest continues on whatever is still owed.

The 2024 reassessment

Augusta reassesses on a five-year cycle. The 2024 reassessment started in September 2022, with notices mailed in February 2024. The county hired Wampler-Eanes Appraisal Group, which split the county into about 96 neighborhoods and visited accessible properties to check records and update property cards and photos.

The county's analysis of 2023 residential sales covered 680 sales. Values rose a median of 58.3 percent over the old assessment, with an average of 60.9 percent. The biggest median increases were in Beverly Manor (69.5 percent) and North River (68.8 percent). The smallest were in Craigsville (33.7 percent, from only three sales) and Wayne (50.9 percent).

A Roanoke or Salem mailing address on a county parcel is common, and it can mislead you about who taxes the house. Roanoke County, Roanoke, Salem and Vinton each have separate rates and offices. Pin down which one bills your parcel before you appeal, pay or request a payoff. The bill itself and the county's parcel records will tell you.

What sellers find in the county

Population stood at 96,929 in 2020, concentrated in suburbs around Roanoke and Salem, with rural, mountainous ground to the north, west and south. Of 42,147 housing units, 5.6 percent sat vacant, and three quarters of occupied units, 75.5 percent, were lived in by their owners. Inherited family houses and downsizing moves are therefore typical reasons to sell.

Interstate 81 and Interstate 581 pass through, along with the Blue Ridge Parkway and a slice of the Jefferson National Forest. Out in the rural parts, a parcel may rely on a private road, a well or a septic system. On Virginia's seller disclosure form the owner makes no statement about wastewater systems, lot lines, easements or special flood hazard areas, and buyers are told to look into them. Having a recent survey, a septic pumping record and a driveway maintenance agreement on hand can rescue a deal.

Own a big parcel? The real estate valuation office can say whether a special land-use program covers it. Changing how land is used can bring additional taxes, and the disclosure form starting January 1, 2027 adds a line about roll-back taxes on land taxed by its use.

At the hearing the proof is on you. The assessor starts out presumed right. Your evidence must outweigh that presumption by showing the value is higher than fair market value, is not uniform with similar property, or was not set using accepted appraisal practice. Note the board is free to raise a figure as well as cut it, in the name of an even tax burden.

  • Sales that closed up to the December 31 before the effective date count, provided you submit them by the locality's cutoff.
  • Studies published after that December 31 are left out.

No. It is an independent city located within the county's borders. Salem hosts the courthouse as county seat, but the county's offices are in the Cave Spring area.

The taxpayer. Virginia Code 58.1-3379 presumes the assessor's value is right, so you need to show it exceeds fair market value or lacks uniformity.

Possibly. A correction request is open for three years after the tax year ends or one year after the assessment, whichever is later, and covers only errors by the assessing office or in a general reassessment.

Neither, directly. Unpaid tax is paid out of the proceeds, which means the seller's share reduces the seller's check. The contract splits the current year.

Fifty cents for every $500 of price. Sellers pay it unless the buyer agrees to, and the clerk collects it at recording.

Virginia puts the real estate tax lien at the front of the line, ahead of every other lien, and keeps it there until the taxing authority has been paid. Generally not for the current bill. Value changes made during the year do not show up on it, because billing is based on January 1, 2026.

Yes. Under section 58.1-3340 of the Code of Virginia, the lien for real estate taxes comes before any other lien or encumbrance until the taxing authority is paid.

Yes. The balance, with penalty and interest, is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, so ask the Treasurer for a written payoff before the closing date.

Culpeper County in brief

Culpeper County covers about 383 square miles of Piedmont country at the base of the Blue Ridge. The seat is the town of Culpeper, and the three smaller towns are Boston, Elkwood and Reva. Population was 52,552 in 2020 and is estimated at 57,666 for 2025. The Rappahannock River forms the northeast border and the Rapidan the south.

Most local workers commute out, chiefly to Fairfax and Fauquier counties, so buyers often shop with the drive in mind. About 72.8 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied. Main routes are US 15, US 29, US 211 and US 522.

Outside the town, communities include Brandy Station, Stevensburg, Jeffersonton, Rixeyville, Lignum and Richardsville. Houses inside the Town of Culpeper carry a town rate on top of the county's.

Tax rate

The county lists a 2026 rate of $0.37 for real estate plus $0.08 for fire and rescue, a total of $0.45 per $100 of assessed value. The Town of Culpeper adds $0.061. Three town service districts add to the town rate: Southridge at $0.03, Lafayette Ridge at $0.035 and Willow Shade at $0.02, as listed under 2025.

The rate changes from year to year, and the list above shows the county total only. Check the final figure with the Treasurer's office before quoting it to a buyer, and remember the town rate and any service district if the house is inside the town.

Due date and where to pay

The county collects once a year, on December 5. Mail your payment to Culpeper County Treasurer, PO Box 1447, Culpeper, VA 22701.

Ask the Treasurer about the penalty and interest before a payment is late. Selling in the fall? Have the closing agent confirm what is paid and how the December bill gets split with the buyer.

How Culpeper reassesses property

Culpeper assesses every two years, on a biennial cycle set by the Board of Supervisors. The current assessment became effective January 1, 2025 and stays in effect until January 1, 2027, with general reassessments falling in odd years.

The Department of Real Estate Assessments uses one or more of three methods:

  • Sales comparison: recent sales of similar properties, adjusted for size, condition, age, location and amenities.
  • Cost: current materials, labor and depreciation, plus the value of comparable vacant land.
  • Income: industry figures on what a property could earn and what it costs to run.

The same office runs the land use program, which must be revalidated at each general reassessment, and tax relief for elderly and disabled owners and certain surviving spouses.

How to appeal your assessment

During a reassessment, the formal route is the Board of Equalization, an independent body appointed by the Circuit Court. It may raise, lower or keep your value.

For each general reassessment the Board of Supervisors fixes when hearings start and the last day to apply, and the Board of Equalization works only in that window. The assessor can give you the dates for the next one.

After that, owners can apply to circuit court. Virginia Code 58.1-3984 lets an aggrieved taxpayer apply within the later of three years from the end of the tax year or one year from the assessment date. The assessor's value is presumed correct for real property.

Using the valuation methods in an appeal

How the county got its number tells you which evidence to bring. Where it leaned on sales comparison, show recent sales of similar houses and note the differences in size, condition, age, location or amenities. If the cost method applies, a repair estimate that shows depreciation or a defect can matter. For a rental, income figures and operating costs speak to the income method.

Photos help under any method, particularly of damage that does not show from the street. Keep a copy of every page you send, with the date.

Land use and relief programs

Two programs at the assessments office can change what a buyer pays. Land use enrollment has to be revalidated at each general reassessment, so if your acreage is in it, learn what a sale does to that status before signing. The same office handles relief for elderly and disabled owners and certain surviving spouses, and it can tell you whether your house is covered.

Working around a single December bill

One bill a year changes how a closing plays out. If you close in spring or summer, the December 5 payment usually falls to the buyer, yet your share of the year is still prorated, so expect to hand the buyer a credit. If you close after December 5, the bill should show as paid, and the closing agent will want the receipt.

Whichever side of the date you are on, get the Treasurer's status in writing and give it to the title company. A missed bill is the one thing that can hold up a settlement over a figure nobody has checked.

Steps before you list

First, find out which rate applies to you: the county total, plus the Town of Culpeper rate and a service district if the house is in one. Second, ask the Treasurer for the paid status of the December 5 bill and for the mailing address for payments. Third, check the assessment, which is in effect from January 1, 2025 until January 1, 2027, and decide whether to wait for the next reassessment before you list. Fourth, ask the assessor about land use enrollment and relief. Finally, choose how to sell: with an agent, or by taking a direct offer on the house as it stands, which skips showings and lender approvals.

Tax and recording costs at closing

Property tax comes first in line. Under Virginia Code 58.1-3340 the lien outranks other liens until the tax is actually paid, sale proceeds must go toward taxes and levies, and a lien reaches the current year's rents too.

On the deed, the state's grantor tax is 50 cents per $500 of consideration (Virginia Code 58.1-802). The seller pays unless the buyer agrees to take it, and the clerk who first records the deed certifies that it was paid.

Selling a Culpeper County house

With one bill a year, the timing of a sale matters. A house that closes before December 5 leaves the question of who pays that bill, and the contract should say. Ask the closing agent to confirm the proration before you sign, and ask the Treasurer whether any earlier year is open.

If the house needs repairs or the commute makes it slow to sell, a direct as-is cash offer skips showings and lender approvals. The tax is still paid from the proceeds at closing, so get a payoff figure first.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Culpeper tax due date?

December 5, once a year. Mail to Culpeper County Treasurer, PO Box 1447, Culpeper, VA 22701.

What is the Culpeper County tax rate for 2026?

$0.37 for real estate and $0.08 for fire and rescue, a total of $0.45 per $100 of assessed value. The Town of Culpeper adds $0.061.

How often does Culpeper County reassess?

Every two years. The current assessment took effect January 1, 2025 and remains until January 1, 2027.

When can I go to the Board of Equalization in Culpeper?

Only in a general reassessment window. The Board of Supervisors sets the dates each time, and the assessor can tell you the next ones.

Does the seller or buyer pay Virginia's grantor tax in Culpeper County?

Normally the seller, at 50 cents for each $500 of consideration, unless both sides agree to a different split.

Fauquier County in brief

Fauquier is a Northern Virginia county of about 651 square miles, mostly open Piedmont land, with Warrenton as its seat. Remington and The Plains are the other towns. The 2020 census counted 72,972 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 76,503. Exurban development from the Washington area has reached parts of the county, including housing along highways in rural areas.

Beyond the towns, many addresses and deeds use unincorporated names such as Bealeton, Calverton, Catlett, Marshall, Midland, New Baltimore, Opal, Paris, Rectortown and Upperville. New Baltimore is the largest community, and the Brookside and Vint Hill subdivisions feed growth in the east. Because 57.5 percent of residents lived in rural areas in 2020, land use rules come up more here than in a city.

Many owners use a Fauquier house as a base for a commute. Fauquier County Public Schools serves most of the county, and the part on Marine Corps Base Quantico belongs to the Defense Department's school system.

Tax rate

The Commissioner of the Revenue's rate page shows a combined real estate rate of $0.895 per $100 of assessed value. That figure is $0.709 base, $0.182 for the fire and rescue levy and $0.004 for the conservation easement fund.

One special district adds to the bill: the Marshall Electric Light and Business Improvement district adds $0.025 per $100. Mobile homes are taxed at the same $0.895 as real estate. Confirm the current-year figure with the office when you plan a sale.

Due dates and payment

The bill comes in two halves, one in June and one in December. Pay the Treasurer's Office, using the county's online tax portal for payments and balances. A date on a weekend moves to the next business day.

Reassessment and appeals

Fauquier reassesses every four years. The last reassessment took effect January 1, 2026, the process carries through 2027, and new values take effect January 1, 2028.

The county's Board of Equalization hears property assessment disputes. The Circuit Court appoints its five members, who must be county residents and a majority freeholders, with at least 30 percent drawn from appraisal, real estate, building, legal or financial work. The deadline to appeal is set by ordinance, so ask the Commissioner's office for the date.

The Commissioner of the Revenue's office is at 10 Courthouse Square, 2nd Floor, Warrenton, VA 20186, phone (540) 422-8880. If the board's result is not enough, you can apply to the circuit court. Virginia Code 58.1-3984 presumes the assessor's value, or the board's adjusted value, is correct and puts the burden on the taxpayer to show the value was wrong and not set under accepted appraisal practice.

Timing a sale around the four-year cycle

Because Fauquier reassesses only every four years, your assessed value stays fixed for a long stretch while the market moves. The 2026 values will stand until the January 1, 2028 values take effect. If prices have climbed since the last reassessment, a buyer may be getting a tax figure that is low compared with a future bill. If prices have slipped, the reverse can be true.

Either way, be ready to explain the number. Give the buyer your assessment, the combined rate of $0.895 per $100, and the date the next values take effect, so they can plan for a change in the bill.

Preparing for a Board of Equalization hearing

Board members are county residents, and a good share come from appraisal, real estate, building, legal or financial work, so a calm, factual case beats anger over a bill. State what you believe the value should be and why. Bring recent sales of similar houses, photos of any defects and repair estimates. Expect the board to begin by assuming the assessor is right, the same starting point a court uses.

If the result is not enough, the next step is the circuit court. Ask the Commissioner's office about the deadline early, since it is set by ordinance and is not repeated on your bill.

Land use and tax relief

The county's use value program taxes qualifying farm, forest, horticultural and open space land by its use, not its market value. If the land stops qualifying, a roll-back assessment applies, and the county requires repayment of the deferred tax plus 10 percent interest for five years plus the current year.

When you sell acreage, ask the Commissioner of the Revenue whether the parcel is in land use before you agree to a closing date, since a change in use can trigger the bill.

The county also offers real estate tax relief for owners age 65 and older or permanently disabled, with reduction or exemption based on income and net worth, applied for each year. The office number for that program is 540-422-8140.

Selling with taxes owed

For a Virginia house, the tax lien stands ahead of the others until it is paid off. Virginia Code 58.1-3340 sends sale proceeds first to taxes and levies on the real estate, with penalties and interest, and leaves the seller's share of the year to the contract.

Recording the deed costs the seller too. The grantor's tax is 50 cents per $500 under Virginia Code 58.1-802, unless the buyer agrees to take it on. Ownership records at the Commissioner's office are updated from deed transfers and other Clerk of the Circuit Court records, so a deed recorded late can mean the wrong person gets billed.

In practice: confirm what is paid with the Treasurer, add up any roll-back that a land use change would trigger, and put both numbers in front of your closing agent a week before the closing date. Ask for the final figures in writing and keep the receipts with your sale papers.

Steps before you sell

Ask the Treasurer which half is paid. Ask the Commissioner of the Revenue whether the land is enrolled in use value and whether relief applies. Decide whether to list now or after the January 1, 2028 values take effect, and look at your current assessment next to what a buyer is likely to pay. Make sure the deed is recorded promptly after closing so the right owner is billed, and keep a copy of the recorded deed with your closing papers.

If the house needs repairs, or you hold acreage with a roll-back risk, an as-is cash offer can avoid showings and lender approvals. Any tax or roll-back still comes out of the proceeds at closing.

What are the Fauquier due dates?

June 5 (first half) and December 5 (second half). A weekend date moves to the next business day.

The five-member Board of Equalization, which the Circuit Court appoints. The Commissioner of the Revenue can give you the filing deadline.

Bedford County in brief

Bedford County covers 769 square miles of Piedmont Virginia, reaching toward the Blue Ridge, with the town of Bedford as the county seat. The 2020 census counted 79,462 residents. Much of the newer housing serves people who commute to Lynchburg or Roanoke or who want to live near Smith Mountain Lake.

The town of Bedford was an independent city from 1968 until it rejoined the county as a town on July 1, 2013. An old deed or letter that mentions the city can confuse things, so ask which office has your parcel on its books. Some unincorporated areas also carry a Bedford or Lynchburg mailing address, which means the address on an envelope may not match the locality that taxes the property. Look for the county name on your bill.

Due dates and payment

Real estate tax comes due twice a year.

You can pay four ways:

  • By mail.
  • In the drop box.
  • In person at the county office, 122 East Main Street, Bedford, VA 24523.

Your bill shows the rate and any late charges; if it does not, call 540-586-7601. Ahead of a sale, ask the treasurer which bills have been paid, because you may have covered only the first half.

The January 2027 reassessment

Bedford is reassessing all real estate, and the new values take effect January 1, 2027. The county hired Wingate Appraisal Service, a firm approved by the Virginia Department of Taxation, to do the work.

Appraisal staff started visiting neighborhoods on March 19, 2025 and were scheduled to keep going for 15 months. They look at the outside of each property, may take photos for internal use only, and leave a flyer when nobody is home. Their vehicles are marked Real Estate Assessment/Wingate Appraisal Service, and staff wear ID badges. If someone shows up without them, call the county.

Virginia law requires localities to bring assessed values up to current market value from time to time, and this is that update. The county said owners would get notices in fall 2026, so watch your mail. Questions go to the Reassessment Office at 540-587-0745.

How to appeal your assessment

The local Board of Equalization hears appeals. Ask the Reassessment Office for the filing window that fits your notice, since it depends on when the notice went out.

Virginia Code section 58.1-3381 requires the board to consider and decide every petition. The board has three options on any value: raise, lower or leave it. An owner gets word before any increase. Virginia Cooperative Extension describes the board stage as taking one to three months.

Still unsettled after the board? Circuit court is next, under section 58.1-3984. The filing window is the later of three years after the end of the tax year or one year after the assessment date, among other listed cases. The court starts from the assumption that the assessor is right, so the owner has to bring more convincing evidence.

  1. Open the notice when it arrives and mark the appeal window.
  2. Call the Reassessment Office with questions about how the value was set.
  3. File with the board if you still disagree.
  4. Go to circuit court only if the board outcome is not acceptable.

Sell before or after the new values apply?

That depends on the number on your notice. A higher assessed value means a bigger bill after January 1, 2027, and a lower one means less. If you are deciding whether to sell, compare the notice with what you expect a buyer to pay.

  • Read the notice as soon as it arrives and note the appeal window.
  • If the value looks wrong, ask the Reassessment Office how a review is requested.
  • Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure for the current year before you close.

Lenders and buyers read the new assessment too, so a high value can complicate a sale even when the house is sound.

Unpaid tax and transfer costs when you sell

Taxes follow the house, not the owner. A lien for unpaid real estate tax sits ahead of other claims under Virginia Code section 58.1-3340, so the closing agent pays it first out of what the buyer sends. Your contract decides how much of this year's bill each side covers.

Virginia caps what a locality may add for lateness at 10 percent of the overdue tax or $10, whichever is more, and 10 percent a year in interest (section 58.1-3916). Bedford's actual terms are a question for the treasurer.

Two deed taxes come up at the table. Section 58.1-802 sets the grantor tax at 50 cents per $500, normally on the seller. Section 58.1-801 sets the recordation tax at 25 cents per $100.

Different questions go to different offices, and calling the right one first saves a week.

  • Treasurer, 540-586-7601: which bills are paid, how to pay, and a payoff figure for closing.
  • Reassessment Office, 540-587-0745: how your 2027 value was set, the appeal window and the review process.
  • County office at 122 East Main Street in Bedford: in-person payments and the drop box.

Jot down the date and who you spoke with. If a title company later questions a figure, you can point to the call.

Steps to sell a Bedford County house

One workable order: confirm on the county records that your parcel is in Bedford County and not the town or Lynchburg; gather recent bills and the assessment notice; request a payoff figure from the treasurer; judge whether the new value is fair enough to leave alone or worth a board filing; then pick a route, either an agent listing or a direct offer.

A listing means repairs, showings and waiting for a buyer's loan to clear. A direct cash offer skips those steps, though the closing agent still collects the tax balance from the proceeds. On either path, put the current year's split in the contract and hold on to proof of payment.

Selling to a cash buyer

Heirs, landlords with a tired rental and owners who now live elsewhere are the usual people who want a quick exit. A coming reassessment, two bills a year and a list of repairs can tip the choice.

June 5 and December 5. Starting in 2026, owners receive two separate bills, one in the spring and one in the fall.

January 1, 2027. The county said notices would go out in fall 2026.

Wingate Appraisal Service, hired by the county and approved by the Virginia Department of Taxation. Call 540-587-0745 with questions.

Is the town of Bedford separate from Bedford County?

It was an independent city from 1968. It went back to town status and rejoined the county on July 1, 2013, and it is the county seat.

Alleghany County at a glance

Virginia's far western edge is where Alleghany County lies, in the top corner of the Roanoke Region. The Allegheny Mountains form its western flank and lend the county its name. Formed on January 5, 1822, from parts of Bath, Botetourt and Monroe counties, it spans 449.7 square miles, about 0.7 percent of them water, and held 15,223 people in 2020. Neighbors are Bath, Rockbridge, Botetourt and Craig counties, plus Monroe and Greenbrier in West Virginia. Near Iron Gate, the Cowpasture and Jackson Rivers meet just beyond the boundary and become the James.

Covington serves as county seat but is an independent city outside the county, so a Covington address may be billed by the city instead of Alleghany County. Look at the bill itself to see which office issued it. Clifton Forge is the biggest town within the county and regained town status on July 1, 2001, with Iron Gate and Low Moor the other places people name most.

Work here depends on a few large employers, such as a paperboard mill in Covington and a rail fueling yard in Clifton Forge, and many residents drive to Lewisburg, Lexington or Roanoke. That keeps the local buyer pool small. Cash buyers can take a house exactly as it stands, which suits owners who would rather not wait on a financed buyer.

Roads and rail

Interstate 64 runs east and west through the county, and U.S. Route 220 runs north and south. Amtrak's Cardinal stops at Clifton Forge, about 12 miles from Covington. With so many residents commuting, buyers weigh interstate access heavily, so spell out your own road access when you speak to one.

Who handles real estate tax

Two Virginia officials split the job. The commissioner of the revenue supervises assessment, and the treasurer sends and collects the bill. Reassessments can come as often as every year or as rarely as every six, and values are generally pegged to January 1. If you think yours is wrong, the local board of equalization is where you take it.

Both offices work out of the county complex at 9212 Winterberry Avenue in Covington. Call them for your current bill, its due date and a figure for what you will owe up to your closing date.

How the Board of Equalization works

This board listens to assessment complaints and may raise, lower or keep an assessment. You can reach it in three ways:

  • Call (540) 863-6640 on a weekday between 8 am and 5 pm, holidays excluded, and book a 15 minute slot.
  • Mail a written complaint to 9212 Winterberry Avenue, Suite E, Covington, VA 24426.
  • Show up at a hearing and speak or hand in written material.

The law assumes the assessment is correct, so the burden is yours. You win by showing it is not uniform with similar properties, backed by substantial evidence, or that it exceeds fair market value. Hearing dates differ from year to year, so ask the county which schedule goes with your notice.

When the board says no

Your last avenue is the circuit court. Section 58.1-3984 of the Virginia Code allows an aggrieved owner to apply there. The deadline is whichever comes later: three years after the tax year ends, or one year after the assessment date, and the statute lists a few other situations.

Courts start from the assessor's figure, or the board's figure if it changed the value, and you carry the burden of proving otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence. A lawsuit rarely makes sense when you are about to sell, since the contract price is what establishes the value.

Back taxes and the closing table

A tax lien sits on the parcel until the taxing authority has been paid, and section 58.1-3340 ranks it ahead of other liens on real estate. No. It is the county seat, yet it is an independent city, and houses inside its limits are handled by the city. Your bill shows which office sent it.

Clifton Forge. It reincorporated as a town within the county on July 1, 2001.

Go to the county Board of Equalization. Phone (540) 863-6640 to book a time, or mail a written complaint to 9212 Winterberry Avenue, Suite E, Covington. Your case has to show the value exceeds market or is out of line with similar properties.

When a house changes hands between installments, someone has to carry the months in between. Your contract sets the split; the settlement agent turns it into line items. Wise County at a glance

Virginia's far southwestern corner, in the Appalachian coalfields beside Kentucky, is where Wise County lies. The seat is the town of Wise, and the biggest town is Big Stone Gap. Where a lender pays your tax, the county sends it a request, provided the tax ticket names the lender. If not, forwarding the bill is your job.

Your first call is to the Commissioner of the Revenue, whose office holds the records and fields assessment questions. The county's real estate page links to a reassessment FAQ. Ask how often the county reassesses and when the appeal windows open this cycle.

Fourth, write down what is wrong with the house, from the roof to the plumbing, so a buyer's offer reflects the real condition.

Mail matters too. Send any change of address to the Treasurer so a final bill is not lost, since a missing bill does not cancel a penalty. If the house has been empty, check that the billing address on file is one you actually read.

With that in hand, you can compare a cash offer with the cost of repairs and the months a listing might take, and decide without pressure.

Coal has driven the local economy since the 1880s, and housing demand still tracks jobs. Families move away or a parent dies, and the house stays empty. That is an ordinary story in this county. Cash buyers can take such a house in the condition it is in, which helps if repairs would cost more than you care to spend.

Commute and schools come up with buyers. The main roads are U.S. Route 23, U.S. Route 58 Alternate, and State Routes 63, 72 and 83. For high schools, the county has Union High in the west, Central High in the central and northern parts, and Eastside High in the east. Knowing these lets you describe the area plainly, and mentioning High Knob and the Clinch River trails never hurts.

On June 10 and November 10. The next day brings a 10% penalty, and interest follows on July 1 and December 1.
